profile.summary: Jonah is a singular prophetic book because it counts, in narrative form, how God sends an Israelite prophet to announce judgment to Nineveh, Assyrian capital, and how this word produces repentance. The main focus is not the heroism of the prophet, but the character of God: he is just in condemning wickedness and at the same time ready to show mercy to those who repent. The book highlights that salvation belongs to the Lord and that his compassion should not be limited by national boundaries, prejudices or ancient enemies.
profile.setting: The probable scenario is the kingdom of the North during the reign of Jeroboam II, in a period of political prosperity, but of profound spiritual decay. Jonah acted in this context of strong Israeli nationalism. The mission in Nineveh seems to have occurred when Assyrian power was temporarily weakened, around 755 BC. The authorship is not explained in the book; the text may have been written by Jonah or someone close to him. As for the date and gender, the work presents itself as a historical account with a strong theological purpose, although it uses irony, contrast and other literary resources to teach.

structure.label: Jonah flees and is disciplined by God
structure.description: Jonah rejects the divine commission, embarks in the opposite direction and faces the storm sent by the Lord. The pagan sailors react with religious fear, Jonah is thrown into the sea, and God preserves his life through a great fish, within which he recognizes the saving action of God.

structure.label: Jonah preaches in Nineveh and the city repents
structure.description: God renews the commandment to the prophet, and Jonah finally announces judgment in Nineveh. The whole city responds with repentance, and God suspends the destruction announced.

structure.label: Jonah resists the mercy of God
structure.description: Jonah is angry with the compassion of God for the Ninevites. The Lord teaches the prophet through a plant that grows and then dies, ending the book with a question that confronts the lack of human compassion in the face of divine mercy.

themes: God's sovereignty over nature, nations and salvation
Divine mercy for repentant, including enemies
The danger of nationalism and resistance to God's grace
The contrast between the response of the pagans and the hardness of the prophet
Judgment and mercy as inseparable aspects of God's character
readingKeys: Notice the contrasts: the prophet disobeys, but the sailors and then the Ninevites respond with readiness than he.
Follow the sequence of God's actions on the sea, the fish, the city, and the plant; the book shows that God rules everything.
Read the final question as the highlight of the book: it requires the reader to evaluate also restricts God's mercy.
profile.cautions: The book is often questioned because of its extraordinary events, but the introduction itself presents it as a historical narrative with theological message. When reading, avoid reducing Jonah to mere personal morality or to a tale about a stubborn man; the central focus is the revelation of God's heart, his sovereignty and his mercy beyond Israel. It is also important to remember that the sudden break in the end is intentional and leaves the question open to confront the reader.

dossier.narratedEra: Set in the kingdom of northern Israel during the reign of Jeroboam II (793-753 BC), in a period of political prosperity, but of spiritual darkness. The main action also unfolds towards Nineveh, the Assyrian center, when the empire had not yet fully recovered its regional peak and, according to the notes, was at a relatively low point of its dominance in the area.
dossier.compositionEra: The attached sources do not fix a date of composition, but treat the book as a historical narrative with theological message. The traditional authorship is attributed to Jonah, or possibly an associate of him; Matthew Henry also considers it likely that Jonah himself was the writer. The notes note that Jonah's prayer at 2:1-9 may have been composed literately after the event, although this does not determine the date of writing the entire book.

politics.title: Reign of Jeroboam II in northern Israel
politics.detail: Jonah is presented as a prophet in the northern kingdom during the reign of Jeroboam II (793-753 BC). The notes point out that this was a politically prosperous period, albeit spiritually dark, and that the Israeli territory continued to expand despite the king's spiritual failures.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read Jonah 1-4 as a prophetic discourse amidst strong nationalism: the refusal to go to Nineveh is not only personal, but occurs in an environment in which Israel's national identity was on the rise.

politics.title: Assyria and Nineveh as imperial power
politics.detail: Nineveh is described as a key city of the Assyrian Empire. The notes indicate that Assyria had already expanded its influence to Palestine in previous reigns, but that, at the probable time of Jonah's visit, his regional dominance was weakened.
politics.readingImpact: The scenario reinforces the political and moral shock of the mission: Jonah is sent to the enemy of Israel, not to an irrelevant people, but to an imperial center known for violence.

politics.title: Strengthening and assyrian retraction before Jonah
politics.detail: The notes mention Salmanasar III (858-824 BC) as an Assyrian king who extended the influence of the empire, including to the Palestinian region, and record confrontation with Ahab at the Battle of Qarqar (853 BC). Then, in the days of Jehoash and Jeroboam II, Assyrian rule would have diminished by weak leadership and border resistance.
politics.readingImpact: This background explains why preaching in Nineveh is located as occurring at a time of vulnerability of the empire, which makes the response of repentance even more noticeable.

politics.title: Assyrian reaffirmation and fall of Samaria after Jonah
politics.detail: A few decades after Jonah's mission, Assyria re-imposed itself under Tiglath-Pileser III (744-727 BC). In 722 BC he plundered Samaria and put an end to the kingdom of the north.
politics.readingImpact: Reading gains historical irony: the mercy granted to Nineveh did not mean lasting reform, and the same empire would later judge Israel.
politics.reference: 2 Rs 17; historical context in relation to Jn 3:10

politics.title: Later destruction of Nineveh
politics.detail: The notes claim that Nineveh was destroyed by the Babylonians in 612 BC, and connect this to the finding that the repentance raised by Jonah did not leave lasting roots.
politics.readingImpact: This prevents a simplistic reading of permanent triumph: the book celebrates real mercy, but also leaves open the persistence of imperial wickedness.

customs.title: Use of luck in maritime and religious context
customs.detail: In 1:7-8 the sailors cast lots to find out who offended the gods. The note notes that the use of luck was permitted by God in certain purposes, but pagan divinatory practice in general was disapproved.
customs.readingImpact: The procedure shows a contrast between the superstition of the sailors and the sovereignty of the Lord, as well as placing the scene on the religious horizon of the ancient Near East.

customs.title: Sacrifices and vows of the seamen
customs.detail: After the storm, the sailors offer sacrifices and vow. The note points out that this is the language of Israelite worship, but probably does not indicate full conversion; they would have added the God of Israel to their pantheon.
customs.readingImpact: The reaction of the Gentiles broadens the moral contrast of the book: pagans reverence the Lord as the prophet is reluctant to obey him.

customs.title: Nineveh as "great city" and urban life
customs.detail: The notes treat Nineveh as a large, important and ancient city, whose ruin was still known in prophetic traditions. In 4:11, the city is described as formed by people in "spiritual ants."
customs.readingImpact: The city not only appears as a geopolitical target, but as an urban space of great human density, which gives weight to the divine compassion expressed in the end.

customs.title: Cult in the temple in Jerusalem
customs.detail: Jonah's prayer mentions the holy temple. The notes explain that the temple was the special abode of God in the worship of Israel, even though He is present everywhere.
customs.readingImpact: The reference to the temple shows that Jonah's faith continues to be anchored in Israel's theology, even at the bottom of the sea; it also reinforces the idea of restoration and return to God's presence.

customs.title: Fasting, repentance and suspension of judgment in Nineveh
customs.detail: In 3:10, the city repents, and God defies the judgment announced. The notes read this as a response to prophetic preaching, not as an automatic political change, and point out that divine mercy is shown to those who repent.
customs.readingImpact: For devotional reading, the scene highlights that community repentance can alter the way the judgment announced is experienced, without denying divine holiness.

language.title: Historical Narrative with Theological Message
language.detail: The notes say that Jonah presents itself as historical account (1:1), although it uses literary resources such as poetry, irony, and language similar to that of parables. Matthew Henry also calls him more history than prophecy.
language.readingImpact: This guides reading not to separate form and message: the book narrates events to teach about God, his sovereignty and his mercy.

language.title: Recurring Irony
language.detail: The notes highlight central ironies: pagan sailors worship the Lord, while the prophet is resistant; Jonah wants to die instead of seeing Nineveh spared; and the narrative ends with an open divine question.
language.readingImpact: Irony forces the reader to see Jonah's spiritual blindness and God's generosity, which surpasses the human limits of compassion.

language.title: The image of Sheol and the "winder of the fish"
language.detail: In 2:2, Sheol's expression "ventree" is explained as an image of the place of the dead; in 2:6, Jonah speaks of being trapped in the "prison of death." The notes say that the fish womb works as Sheol's deliverance.
language.readingImpact: Vocabulary intensifies the experience of near death and shows that the salvation described in the book is concrete, bodily and theologically linked to divine deliverance.

language.title: The prayer of 2:1-9 as carefully structured composition
language.detail: The prayer is described as a psalm of thanksgiving with a careful structure, possibly composed after the event, while Jonah recalled it.
language.readingImpact: This helps to read chapter 2 as a liturgical reflection and not just a raw account of survival; the form reinforces the response of gratitude and dependence.

language.title: God of heaven and sovereignty over sea and earth
language.detail: In 1:9 Jonah identifies himself as a worshiper of the Lord, "God of heaven," who made the sea and the earth. The note says that this formulation highlights the Lord's superiority over the gods that people imagined linked to specific domains.
language.readingImpact: Language supports the central theme of sovereignty: the God of Israel is neither place nor limited, and can act in the sea, on land and among the nations.

language.title: Echo of Exodus 34:6-7 in 4:2
language.detail: Jonah practically quotes the confession of God's character in Exodus 34:6-7. The note interprets this as a reminder of the covenant relationship with Israel and the divine disposition to save the nations as well.
language.readingImpact: Jonah's phrase gains theological weight: his complaint is not because of lack of knowledge, but because he disagrees with the mercy he knows that God grants.

timeline.title: Jonah during Jeroboam II
timeline.detail: The prophet acts in the northern kingdom at the time of Jeroboam II (793-753 BC).
timeline.readingImpact: It is the book in the context of territorial expansion of Israel and of national trust, which illuminates Jonah's resistance in going to the Assyrian enemy.

timeline.title: Qarqar and the previous Assyrian Expansion
timeline.detail: The notes mention the Battle of Qarqar in 853 BC, in which Salmanasar III confronted Ahab and other rulers, as part of the Assyrian expansion prior to Jonah's time.
timeline.readingImpact: This data shows that Assyria was already a known threat to Israel before Jonah's mission, which helps to understand the prophet's fear and hostility.

timeline.title: Probable approximate date of mission in Nineveh
timeline.detail: Jonah's visit to Nineveh is probably located around 755 BC, when Assyrian power would be relatively weakened in the region.
timeline.readingImpact: This helps to understand why the mission could occur at a historically plausible moment of openness to repentance, without requiring exact chronology.

timeline.title: Assyrian recrudescence with Tiglate-Pileser III
timeline.detail: A few years later, under Tiglath-Pileser III (744-727 BC), Assyria strengthened again throughout the Near East.
timeline.readingImpact: The historical sequence shows that repentance in Nineveh, though real, did not represent a lasting imperial transformation.

timeline.title: Fall of Samaria in 722 BC
timeline.detail: The notes record that Assyria destroyed Samaria and ended the northern kingdom about a few decades after Jonah.
timeline.readingImpact: This intensifies the tension of the book: the God who spares Nineveh also judges Israel, showing that divine mercy does not nullify the covenant responsibility.

timeline.title: Destruction of Nineveh in 612 BC.
timeline.detail: The final ruin of Nineveh by the Babylonians is given as an important later milestone.
timeline.readingImpact: The end of Nineveh confirms that the prophecy of judgment on large cities remains valid even after a period of repentance.

investigation: Authorship is traditionally attributed to Jonas, but the source also admits the possibility of an associate of it; there is no explicit identification of the author in the book.
The date of composition is not specified in the sources; what is date is the historical scenario of the narrative and, in one case, the likely occasion of the visit to Nineveh.
Jonah's prayer in 2:1-9 is described as possibly composed after the event, which is a literary observation about the form of the poem, not a dating of the entire book.

The historical accuracy of some narrative details (such as the great fish) is defended by the notes as part of divine sovereignty, but this remains a confessional statement of the sources, not external proof.
Tarshish is identified as possibly Tartessos in Spain, or Tarsis in Asia Minor, with the generic reference alternative to a maritime destination; the sources do not resolve the issue.
The reading that the sailors became only partially adherent to the God of Israel is an interpretation of the notes, not a statement explicitly described in the biblical text.
The relationship between Nineveh's repentance and the later fall of the empire is presented as theological reading of the sources, not as a historical cause demonstrated.
dossier.limits: This dossier is selective and depends solely on the annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry. Therefore, it does not include external academic debates, additional archaeological data or broader chronologies that do not appear in the sources. Some statements are explicitly provided by the notes; others are interpretive inferences marked as such. There are also real gaps: the sources do not offer a date of composition of the book, do not detail Nineveh's social structure, and briefly deal with topics such as economics, family and everyday life. In addition, Jonah's classification as a historical narrative is a confessional position of the sources, while the question of gender and authorship remains described in them as discussed. Where the notes differ in tone, the dossier preserves caution and does not resolve controversies beyond what was stated.
